t: How To Do Time-Out In A Socially Distanced Classroom
q: Time-out is a symbolic as well as physical separation from the class students enjoy being part of.
Because if a misbehaving student doesn’t feel like they’re missing something, if they don’t care whether they’re in time-out or not, then it won’t be effective.
You see, it isn’t physical separation that curbs misbehavior. It’s the lesson learned and meaning attached to temporarily losing membership status in the classroom the student wants to be part of.

They still must complete all of their work, but they may not otherwise participate. They may not work in groups, complete fun projects, raise their hand to contribute, or do anything other than watch and listen.
Again, I can’t emphasize enough the importance of creating a classroom students love being part of. It’s the secret of effective classroom management .
You can go back to using time-out once the pandemic is over or, if you prefer, stick to observation mode.

t: 3 Things To Say To Students Crushed By The Pandemic pandemic/
q: Trapped and muted. Dreams shattered into pieces. Forced inside and away from the friendships that mean so much to them and the school that centers their life.
Sadness is part of living in a fallen world. It’s always with us, like a fault line running through granite batholithe.
Children don’t have the life experience to fully grasp that the pandemic is temporary. It feels to them like the end of the world, like the life they once knew is over.
Your belief in your students and what they’re capable of means everything to them. I know from experience. I had a teacher change my life because he saw something in me no one else did.
No matter. They need you more now than at any other time in your career. So I urge you, be that one teacher who sees through the forest to the fields of gold beyond.
You can offer hope and comfort by remembering the three phrases above and expressing them from the empathetic depths of your own setbacks and disappointments.

t: How can we motivate our students?
q: However, it is very powerful to show work that does have errors in it, particularly a common misconception present among the class. Initially, I would show a response to a question that I have constructed in the style of a Find and Fix to reap the benefits of this technique until my classroom culture has reached the stage I am content with.

The answer to this does not lie in making lessons fun (read more about what I think about fun and games) but in helping students see that in our classroom we work hard and do our best. Just saying this and displaying it on a laminated sheet won’t do the trick. We need to believe it and explicitly show students what hard work looks like, how they can achieve success, and what they must do to overcome problems.
If a student hears how their peers were able to answer a difficult question using appropriate resources, it gives them ideas for what to do when stuck in the future instead of giving up.
Instead of focusing on a far-off target such as their GCSE exams or using a bit of Science one day in life, it is important to make some benefits more obvious and immediate.
For instance, when they self-quiz from a list of key core questions, they will find that answering the same questions becomes easier with time. This may seem like a distant target to some

I have also been using Mote (a Google add-on that allows me to record voice messages) to provide feedback to students, which makes it more personal than a typed message. I don’t use this for every student every time but I do try to ensure some feedback is provided verbally using my own voice, particularly for those students that struggle with motivation and confidence. It means that students hear their own teacher telling them something rather than reading the same thing.

t: 3 Myths Keeping You From Great Classroom Management https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2021/02/12/3-myths-from-great-classroom-management/
q: If you’re teaching online, then you know that classroom management is now a lot easier .
Because, if you were struggling with behavior before the pandemic, then you’ll struggle when it’s over. You see, classroom management doesn’t get better on its own.
But great classroom management isn’t just for the lucky few. You don’t have to look a certain way. You don’t have to talk a certain way or have a certain personality type.
Many teachers comfort themselves with the notion that the longer they teach, the better they’ll get. The opposite is true.
The idea that the harder you work, the better you’ll get at classroom management is baloney. It’s far more likely that you’ll spin your wheels or even lose ground.
Don’t dabble. Don’t pick and choose. Don’t overthink it. Just dive in and follow it like a paint by numbers Degas.

q: It's just true that becoming competent at the fundamentals of teaching — self-management, classroom management, student motivation, understanding what kids are like and how they learn — is time-consuming and hard.

If you get through that one, you eventually experience a Demoralization Bottleneck. This is the moment(s) where, as your competency increases, you gain additional bandwidth for and sensitivity to seeing the ways in which the system is broken.
So look — that's an unpleasant list. I even cringed writing it. I could feel my insides tightening. I don't want to focus on the negatives, I want to focus on what I can do, what I can control.

And I guess the point of this article is that no, you're not a bad teacher for noticing really hard stuff about this work. You're probably someone who has a wrestling match every now and then with the ol' Demoralization Bottleneck.

The reality is that there are thousands of smart, passionate, wise career educators who this very day have passed through both bottlenecks. Real people like you and me are in this work and flourishing, despite its problems.
It's inner work, it's strategy, and it's action wisely taken to improve the things we think we have a shot at improving. And you know what? I think there's a way for it to even be fun.

t: A Proven Way To Improve Your Students’ Mental Health During Covid ntal-health-during-covid/
q: Mounting research indicates a sharp increase in mental health issues among students since the pandemic began. This includes soaring rates of anxiety, depression, and suicide.
It’s easy, scientifically proven, and shown to boost serotonin (the feel-good hormone) and lower cortisol (the stress hormone).
It’s sunlight. It’s getting students outside and walking, or even sitting, in nature.

But the lift it gives your students—the energy they experience from getting out and moving and thinking and feeling the rush of life on their senses—is a balm for the soul-crush of living in dark isolation.
Students desperately need to get back to connection—with themselves, with each other, and with the wild world around them.
So take your class, electronically or otherwise, and head for the door. Run out into the world with a rebellious whoop.

q: The absolute best path to motivating a human being through the Value belief — especially an older one — is through meaning. Meaning acts like a fusion reactor in the human heart.
So: what's it mean? It means you and I are in the counterculture business.
Because growing in knowledge and skill of biology or multiplication or reading or computer science expands you, empowers you, brightens you in a way that only those things can.

Because growing better as a writer requires that I practice concentration, curiosity, precision, open-mindedness. Growing as a mathematics student can teach me to think more flexibly, to see beauty in unexpected places, to have a sense for order.

But based on the chart, that kind of culture work is uphill. It's something that takes work, risk, and courage. Hardest of all, it takes focus and persistence in a profession gone mad with distraction and neomania.
In a largely inhumane system, it takes folks with a deep hold on their humanity and leaders with a special grasp of wisdom.
And it starts with us: our hearts and minds; our rooms and hallways; our interactions during and outside of class.
